Rockfish.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Rockfish in Hoke County, where Sandhills west of Fayetteville puts woods and water right against housing. Raccoons den in chimneys and attics in spring, squirrels chew soffits year-round, and bats use older rooflines in summer.

Most Rockfish jobs start with a full roofline, attic, and crawlspace inspection, then removal and sealing as one job, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Rockfish is a Sandhills community, and sand is the story of its wildlife work. The deep sandy soil of Hoke County tunnels easily and drains fast: eastern moles run it everywhere, groundhogs and armadillos dig it at every slab and porch, and the longleaf pine and scrub oak woods that surround the community's subdivisions keep raccoons, gray squirrels, and opossums in constant circulation. Rockfish has grown fast as Fort Liberty families have spread west of Fayetteville, and the pattern repeats on every new street — houses finished last year, woods at the back fence, and animals testing the new construction before the landscaping is in.

New construction carries a particular Rockfish risk: the houses are tight, but the sites are not. Builders' debris piles, ungraded sand, open crawlspace vents on the pier-built homes, and garage corners that never quite meet the slab are the first-year entries, and the animals find them in the first season. Our Rockfish inspections give new homes the full read anyway — 'new' describes the framing, not the site — and give the older farmhouses and mill-era homes along the community's rural roads the deep version: outbuildings, well houses, and the barn-adjacent chimneys raccoons prefer.
Rockfish.extendedBody:
Sandhills ground work: moles, armadillos, and the slab edge

In Rockfish the ground calls outnumber the roof calls. Moles tunnel the deep sand in systems that surface across entire yards; armadillos — well established in the Sandhills now — root the same ground for grubs and dig their burrows under porches, driveways, and AC pads; groundhogs hold the sunny field edges and road banks. Our ground work combines trapping the animals working your property with closing what they dug: burrow openings backfilled and screened, because in sand this loose an open burrow is re-let within weeks. We are also straight about moles: a mole job is a campaign over the active tunnel system, not a single visit, and we set that expectation before we set the first trap.

Who is credentialed to do this work in North Carolina

Our Rockfish operators are licensed Wildlife Control Agents with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission, and removal runs through the depredation-permit system — the permit your agent issues for your property, naming the species. It is the credential that matters in this state, and it carries the state's rules with it, including the bat calendar: evictions are prohibited during pup season, May 1 through July 31. Rockfish's older homes hold big brown bat colonies in their attics; found in the window, a colony is mapped and staged, then excluded completely when the season opens.

Fort Liberty growth and the first-year house

For the new subdivisions, the advice is a first-year inspection even when nothing has been heard yet: crawlspace vents screened, garage corners checked, the debris and grade issues at the back lot line flagged. It is the cheapest visit in this business, and in a community growing into longleaf woods, it is the one that prevents the second-year attic colony.
